passage: The substitute teacher had stepped out, and Class 6C at Hill View School grew loud in seconds. A group near the window started chanting "Chashmish! Chashmish!" at Hrithik, who had just got thick new glasses. Parul, eleven, never teased anyone; she was the girl who lent pencils. But everyone was laughing, the noise was huge, and nobody would notice one more voice. She joined in, quietly at first, then loudly. It felt oddly easy, as if the voice wasn't hers. Hrithik pushed his glasses up and stared at his desk, ears red. Then the door opened and the class teacher walked in. The chant died. She looked straight at Parul. "You too?" Parul's stomach dropped. Alone, under that look, she could hardly believe she'd done it. At recess the teacher sat with Hrithik, and Parul went over to say sorry.

qa.a: Hrithik felt humiliated and alone, staring at his desk with red ears while the whole class seemed against him.

qa.a: Mehak felt annoyed and defensive, sure her new role justified what she did.

qa.q: What could Mehak do if she wanted to stay the same person as a lead?
qa.a: She could apply the same rules to herself, credit Divyansh for his research, and ask how juniors are doing, not just what they owe.

qa.q: How might Divyansh feel walking back to his desk?
qa.a: Divyansh likely felt hurt and unheard, since Mehak ignored both his mother's appointment and his work.

grounding: A lead intern with some authority stops noticing juniors' feelings and bends rules for herself, while believing she hasn't changed.

passage: When I became hostel secretary in second year, I honestly thought I was the same person. I'm Disha. But looking back, I can see the slide. I stopped queueing for the washing machine; I had "duties." I let my friends stay past curfew and wrote up juniors who did the same. When Dilnaz, a first-year, came to me because her roommate's music kept her awake before exams, I told her to "adjust." I remember thinking she was being dramatic. Later I found out she'd been crying most nights. The worst part was that I didn't notice any of it at the time. I just felt busy and important. It was only when my old friend said, "You used to ask people how they were," that I felt the floor tilt.

qa.q: What did Disha tell Dilnaz to do?
qa.a: Disha told her to "adjust."

qa.q: How did Disha feel when the old friend spoke up?
qa.a: Disha felt shaken and ashamed, as if the floor tilted, realising how much had changed.

qa.q: What could have kept Disha from drifting?
qa.a: Keeping the same rules for Disha and friends as for juniors, and regularly asking juniors how they were, might have kept her empathy.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz have experienced being told to adjust?
qa.a: Dilnaz probably felt dismissed and alone, which is why she was crying most nights.

grounding: A former hostel secretary looks back on how authority made the secretary less attentive to juniors and quicker to bend rules, without noticing at the time.

passage: In the Osaka office, Felix, twenty-four, had learnt to read Yuki's footsteps. Quick and heavy meant a bad morning; everyone kept their heads down. Slow meant she might be open to ideas. In meetings he watched her face before speaking. Once, early on, he'd pointed out a flaw in her plan, and she'd gone silent and cold for a week. Since then, when she asked, "Any thoughts?" Felix said, "It looks good." He had thoughts. He wrote them in a notebook he never showed anyone. At night, on the train home, he felt smaller than when he'd arrived in Japan: less funny, less sure. His friends back in Berlin asked why he never posted anymore. He didn't know how to explain that he'd forgotten what his own opinions sounded like out loud.

qa.q: What did quick and heavy footsteps mean?
qa.a: Quick and heavy meant a bad morning.

qa.q: What was Felix feeling on the train home?
qa.a: Felix felt small and unsure, less like himself after months of hiding his views.

qa.q: What small step could help Felix?
qa.a: Felix could share one idea at a time with a trusted colleague or through a written suggestion, rebuilding his voice without risking a big confrontation.

qa.q: How might Yuki see Felix's constant "It looks good"?
qa.a: Yuki may think he agrees with her and never realise how much he holds back out of fear.

grounding: A junior employee learns to read a powerful manager's moods and hide his views, and feels smaller for it.

passage: At the bank branch in Kanpur, the manager Yusuf-sir's cabin had glass walls, and every junior watched them. Sachin, twenty-five, had worked there a year. He knew that if Yusuf-sir tapped his pen, it was a bad day. If he loosened his tie, you could ask for leave. Sachin never said no in meetings. When Yusuf-sir proposed pushing a loan product that Sachin thought confused customers, Sachin nodded and said, "Very good idea, sir." At lunch, the other juniors whispered their real opinions, then went quiet when the cabin door opened. Sachin noticed he'd started talking less at home too. His wife asked why he seemed so quiet. He said he was tired. Really, he felt like he'd shrunk, and the only thing he'd grown was his ability to guess another man's mood.

qa.q: What did it mean if Yusuf-sir tapped his pen?
qa.a: It was a bad day.

qa.q: How was Sachin feeling when he said "Very good idea, sir"?
qa.a: Sachin felt uneasy and small, hiding his real doubts out of fear of the manager's reaction.

qa.q: What could help Sachin keep some voice at work?
qa.a: He could raise concerns in writing with facts about customer confusion, or find a fair senior he trusts to talk to.

qa.q: How might Sachin's wife see the change in him?
qa.a: His wife notices he has grown quiet and may feel worried or shut out, not knowing the cause.

grounding: A junior bank employee learns to read his manager's moods, hides his views and says only what pleases, and feels smaller.

passage:
Dear Jeevan,
You asked why I sound so flat on our calls. It's work. My manager at the agency is brilliant, and everyone's scared of her. I've learnt the signs: if she sighs before a meeting, don't pitch anything new. If she smiles, it's safe to ask for a day off. I plan my whole week around her face.
Last month I had a campaign idea I really believed in. I brought it up, she frowned, and I said "Or we could do it your way." I didn't even finish explaining.
The worst part isn't her. It's me. I used to argue with professors. Now I say "absolutely" twenty times a day. I feel smaller every month.
Can we talk on Sunday? Not about work. About what I used to be like.
Himani

qa.q: What does Himani say twenty times a day?
qa.a: Himani says "absolutely" twenty times a day.

qa.q: How does Himani feel about the change in Himani's own behaviour?
qa.a: Himani feels flat and diminished, more upset by Himani's own silence than by the manager.

qa.q: What could Himani do to reclaim some voice?
qa.a: Himani could talk things through with Jeevan, then try sharing one idea fully, perhaps in writing, rather than giving up before finishing.

qa.q: How might Jeevan feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Jeevan might feel worried for Himani and eager to remind Himani of the confident person from before.

grounding: A junior employee learns to read a powerful manager's moods, hides personal views and feels smaller while saying only what pleases.

passage: Kofi and Emeka had joined the Accra design firm the same month and shared lunch every day for two years. Then Emeka became team manager. Over three months, Kofi watched him change. Emeka started interrupting people in meetings, took the best desk by the window, and expected juniors to fetch his coffee. At lunch he checked his phone while Kofi talked. Kofi heard others gossiping. He didn't join. One evening, walking to the bus, he said, "Emeka, can I say something as your friend? You've stopped listening in meetings. People notice." Emeka bristled. "You don't know the pressure I'm under." Kofi nodded. "I believe you. The pressure's real. I just miss how you used to hear people out." Emeka was quiet all the way to the stop.

qa.q: What did Emeka take after becoming manager?
qa.a: He took the best desk by the window.

qa.q: What was Kofi feeling as he watched Emeka change?
qa.a: Kofi felt sad and concerned, missing his friend and uneasy about how others were treated.

qa.q: Which part of Kofi's approach worked, and why?
qa.a: He named the change privately as a friend and acknowledged the pressure, which made it easier for Emeka to hear rather than feel attacked.

qa.q: How might Emeka have felt when Kofi spoke to him?
qa.a: Emeka felt defensive at first, but his silence to the bus stop suggests he was thinking it over.

grounding: A peer watches a friend become a manager and stop listening, and gently names the change while acknowledging pressure, instead of gossiping.

passage: At the Pune logistics office, Joseph watched Tanvir take over as shift manager. They'd been friends since induction, cracking jokes over vada pav at the gate. Within two months, Tanvir started cutting people off mid-sentence, skipped the joint tea break, and expected the team to cover his late arrivals without a word. The team grumbled in the washroom. Joseph felt a pull to join them; it would have been easy. Instead, one night after the shift, he found Tanvir alone at the loading bay. "Tanvir, you've started talking over people. I don't think you mean to." Tanvir stiffened. "Head office is on my neck every day, Joseph." "I know. That's real. But the guys feel you've stopped hearing them." Tanvir exhaled, then said, "Tell me when I do it again." Joseph said he would.

qa.q: Where did Joseph find Tanvir alone?
qa.a: Joseph found Tanvir alone at the loading bay.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling when the team grumbled in the washroom?
qa.a: Joseph felt tempted to join the gossip but uneasy, caring about Tanvir too much to talk behind his back.

qa.q: Why was talking to Tanvir alone better than gossiping?
qa.a: It gave Tanvir honest, private feedback he could act on, while showing understanding of his pressure.

qa.q: How did Tanvir respond to Joseph's words?
qa.a: Tanvir was defensive at first, citing head office pressure, but then asked Joseph to tell him when he did it again, showing openness.

grounding: A peer sees a friend become a manager and stop listening, and gently names the change in private while acknowledging the pressure.

passage:
Dear Gurleen,
I've been meaning to write for weeks, and I'd rather say this kindly than let it grow.
Since you became team lead, I've noticed small changes. You interrupt in meetings more. You don't join us for lunch. Last Friday, when Anil raised a concern, you said, "Just do it," and moved on. And you expect us to adjust around your schedule, which the old Gurleen would never have done.
I'm not writing because I'm angry. I know the pressure from the directors must be enormous; I've seen you working at midnight. It would change anyone.
But I miss the colleague who used to say, "Wait, let's hear everyone." I think the team does too. I'm telling you because you're my friend, not to complain.
Lunch on Monday?
Devika

qa.q: What did Gurleen say when Anil raised a concern?
qa.a: Gurleen said, "Just do it," and moved on.

qa.q: What is Devika feeling while writing the letter?
qa.a: Devika feels caring but concerned, missing the old colleague and not wanting resentment to grow.

qa.q: Why might Devika's letter work better than gossip?
qa.a: It names specific changes kindly and privately, acknowledges the pressure, and invites reconnection, instead of gossiping.

qa.q: How might Gurleen react to the letter?
qa.a: Gurleen might feel stung at first, then perhaps grateful that a friend chose honesty over talking behind Gurleen's back.

grounding: A peer writes to a friend who became team lead, gently naming how the friend stopped listening, while acknowledging the pressure of the role.

passage: The monsoon had flooded half the villages the NGO served, and Hafsa, twenty-five, had just been made field lead. The relief plan had to be finalised by noon. She could have written it alone; the director trusted her. Instead she called the field workers together in the leaky office. "Tell me what's wrong with my plan. Honestly." Pankaj, who'd been there longer than her, frowned. "You've sent the trucks to the main road. The hamlets past the river are cut off. We'd have to carry supplies on foot." Hafsa felt a flash of irritation, then asked, "What would that cost your team?" "Four extra hours. But the hamlets need it most." She changed the plan. When the director praised it that evening, Hafsa said, "Pankaj caught the gap. The credit's his."

qa.q: How many extra hours would carrying supplies on foot take?
qa.a: Four extra hours.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling when Pankaj criticised the plan?
qa.a: Hafsa felt a flash of irritation but stayed curious, choosing to listen rather than defend her plan.

qa.q: Which of Hafsa's habits guards against self-importance, and why?
qa.a: She invited honest criticism, asked what her decision cost the team and shared credit, which kept her attentive to others.

qa.q: How might Pankaj feel when Hafsa credited him to the director?
qa.a: Pankaj likely felt respected and valued, more willing to speak up again.

grounding: A young leader invites honest feedback, asks what her decision costs those below her and shares credit, staying curious about others under time pressure.

passage: Tarun, twenty-six, had just become the youngest team lead at his Bengaluru start-up. On his first day, he did something unusual: he took his old friend Kiran for chai and said, "You're the one person who'll tell me when I'm being an idiot. Please keep doing it." Kiran laughed. "Easy." Three weeks later, Tarun pushed a deadline that meant the team would work through a weekend. Kiran caught him at the lift. "You're being an idiot. Half the team has family events." Tarun's pride flared. Then he remembered his own request. He asked the team directly what the weekend would cost them. It was a lot. He moved the deadline by four days and told the client himself. At the next review he named two juniors whose work had saved the project. Kiran raised his cup across the room.

qa.q: By how many days did Tarun move the deadline?
qa.a: He moved the deadline by four days.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling when Kiran called him an idiot at the lift?
qa.a: Tarun felt a flare of wounded pride, then remembered his request and chose to listen.

qa.q: Why was asking Kiran to keep telling him the truth a wise move?
qa.a: Keeping a friend who will disagree helps Tarun notice when power starts making him careless about others.

qa.q: How might the juniors feel when Tarun named them at the review?
qa.a: The juniors likely felt proud and valued, seeing their lead share credit publicly.

grounding: A young team lead keeps a friend who will disagree, asks what his deadline costs the team, and shares credit, limiting the drift toward self-importance.

passage:
"Trisha, got a minute before service?"
"Sure, chef." Trisha wiped her hands.
"You've been on this line three years. I got head chef two weeks ago. What am I doing badly?"
Trisha blinked. "Honestly?"
"That's the only way I want it."
"You changed the prep schedule without asking. Now the morning crew comes in an hour earlier and nobody told them why."
Rehana winced. "What did that cost them?"
"Buses. Kids' school drop. Suresh has been coming in late and getting shouted at."
"By me."
"By you."
Rehana was quiet. "Okay. I'll talk to the crew today and we'll fix the schedule together. And Trisha, tell me again when I mess up."
"You really want that?"
"I really need that." Rehana smiled. "Also, your sauce idea from Tuesday? I'm putting your name on the menu."

qa.q: How long has Trisha been on the line?
qa.a: Trisha has been on this line three years.

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling when she heard about Suresh?
qa.a: Rehana felt uncomfortable and regretful, realising her schedule change had hurt the crew.

qa.q: Which of Rehana's actions show humility safeguards?
qa.a: She asked for honest feedback, asked what her decision cost the crew, planned to fix it together, and put Trisha's name on the menu.

qa.q: How might Trisha feel about being asked for honesty?
qa.a: Trisha was surprised at first but likely felt trusted and respected by the new head chef.

grounding: A young head chef invites honest feedback, asks what her decision costs her staff, and shares credit to guard against self-importance.
